sceneHappening: The twelve sent out, five thousand fed, the transfiguration, and Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem
summary: Jesus gives the twelve power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them to proclaim the Kingdom of God and heal. "Take nothing for your journey, neither staff, nor wallet, nor bread, nor money; neither have two coats apiece." Herod the tetrarch hears of all this and is perplexed: John was beheaded, so "who is this about whom I hear such things?" He tries to see him. When the apostles return and tell what they have done, Jesus takes them privately to a town called Bethsaida, but the crowds follow. He welcomes them, speaks of the Kingdom of God, and heals. As evening comes, the twelve ask him to send the crowd away to find food, and he says, "You give them something to eat." With five loaves and two fish he has them sit in groups of about fifty, blesses and breaks the food, and gives it to the disciples to set before the people; all eat, and twelve baskets of broken pieces remain. After Jesus has been praying alone, he asks, "Who do the multitudes say that I am?" John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. "But who do you say that I am?" Peter says, "The Christ of God." Jesus warns them to tell no one, and says the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, be killed, and be raised on the third day. "If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me." About eight days later he takes Peter, John, and James up on the mountain to pray, and as he prays his face changes and his clothing becomes dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appear in glory and speak of his departure, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The three are heavy with sleep, but staying awake they see his glory. As the two leave, Peter says, "Master, it is good for us to be here; let's make three tents," not knowing what he says. A cloud overshadows them, and a voice says, "This is my Son, my chosen. Listen to him." Jesus is found alone, and they keep silent. Next day a man from the crowd begs Jesus to look at his only child, a boy seized by a spirit that convulses and shatters him. The disciples couldn't drive it out. Jesus says, "Faithless and perverse generation, how long will I be with you?" and heals the boy, giving him to his father. While everyone marvels, he says again that the Son of Man will be delivered into men's hands, but they don't understand it, and are afraid to ask. They argue about who is greatest, and he sets a child by him: "Whoever receives this little child in my name receives me ... for whoever is least among you all, the same is great." John says they stopped someone casting out demons in his name, and Jesus says, "Don't forbid him, for he who is not against you is for you." As the days are fulfilled for him to be received up, he "sets his face" to go to Jerusalem and sends messengers ahead, who enter a Samaritan village; they do not receive him because his face is set toward Jerusalem. James and John ask, "Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky, and destroy them?" He rebukes them and they go to another village. On the road someone says, "I will follow you wherever you go." Jesus says, "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." To another he says, "Follow me," and the man asks first to bury his father: "Leave the dead to bury their own dead, but you go and announce the Kingdom of God." A third wants to say goodbye at home: "No one, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, is fit for the Kingdom of God."
whySettingMatters: Luke 9 is the hinge of the book. Peter's confession and the first prediction of suffering begin the turn toward Jerusalem, and "he set his face" (9:51) starts the long travel narrative that runs to 19:44. Luke's phrase "his departure" in 9:31 is the Greek word exodos, so the conversation with Moses and Elijah is about a new exodus accomplished at Jerusalem. "Received up" in 9:51 covers death, resurrection, and ascension together. Luke's Herod, the tetrarch Antipas, is perplexed rather than fearful as in Mark. The feeding takes place near Bethsaida, in a deserted place; groups of fifty recall Israel's camp organization in the wilderness. Samaritans and Jews were divided over where to worship (Gerizim or Jerusalem), and pilgrims heading for Jerusalem were often unwelcome in Samaria; James and John's request recalls Elijah calling fire down (2 Kings 1:10-12). "Burying my father" most likely refers to a continuing duty to the family; the claim that the father had already died is debated, but the point is the claim of the kingdom. Elisha was called while plowing and allowed to say goodbye (1 Kings 19:19-21), and Jesus asks for more. Foxes and birds have homes, a way of saying he has none.

questions: Peter says "The Christ of God" and Jesus immediately talks about suffering. What is the connection?
On the mountain, Moses and Elijah speak of Jesus' "departure." What does the word exodus add?
Luke says Jesus "set his face" toward Jerusalem. What does that say about how he goes?
Three people offer to follow, and Jesus answers each with a hard word. What is he testing?
